# Data import and understanding

I loaded the two datasets and checked their columns and sizes.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
pop_raw <- read.csv("data/world_population.csv", check.names=TRUE)
co2_raw <- read.csv("data/CO2_emission.csv", check.names=TRUE)
cat("Population:", nrow(pop_raw), "rows and", ncol(pop_raw), "columns\n")
cat("CO2:", nrow(co2_raw), "rows and", ncol(co2_raw), "columns\n")
cat("Population columns:\n"); print(names(pop_raw))
cat("CO2 columns:\n"); print(names(co2_raw))
knitr::kable(head(pop_raw, 5), caption="First five population rows")
knitr::kable(tail(pop_raw, 10), caption="Last ten population rows")
str(pop_raw)
```

# Exploratory data analysis and cleaning

## Missing values and duplicates

```{r}
quality <- data.frame(Dataset=c("Population","CO2"),
 Rows=c(nrow(pop_raw),nrow(co2_raw)),
 Columns=c(ncol(pop_raw),ncol(co2_raw)),
 Duplicate_rows=c(sum(duplicated(pop_raw)),sum(duplicated(co2_raw))),
 Missing_cells=c(sum(is.na(pop_raw)),sum(is.na(co2_raw))))
knitr::kable(quality, caption="Initial data quality")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable=names(pop_raw), Missing=colSums(is.na(pop_raw))), caption="Population missingness by variable")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable=names(co2_raw), Missing=colSums(is.na(co2_raw))), caption="CO2 missingness by variable")
```

## Clean the data

I removed the repeated 2019 column. I only estimated short gaps between known CO2 values. I kept the other missing values and used the original 2019 data for the main analysis.

```{r}
pop_clean <- unique(pop_raw)
co2_clean <- unique(co2_raw)
if ("X2019.1" %in% names(co2_clean)) {
  if (identical(co2_clean$X2019, co2_clean$X2019.1)) {
    co2_clean$X2019.1 <- NULL
  }
}
co2_years <- 1990:2019
co2_cols <- paste0("X", co2_years)

# Fill only short missing gaps between known years
fill_short_gaps <- function(x, max_gap=2) {
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  known <- which(!is.na(x))
  if (length(known) < 2) return(x)
  estimated <- approx(x=known, y=x[known], xout=seq_along(x), rule=1)$y
  missing <- which(is.na(x))
  if (!length(missing)) return(x)
  runs <- split(missing, cumsum(c(1, diff(missing)!=1)))
  for (r in runs) {
    if (length(r) <= max_gap && min(r)>min(known) && max(r)<max(known)) x[r] <- estimated[r]
  }
  x
}
co2_interpolated <- co2_clean
co2_interpolated[co2_cols] <- t(apply(co2_clean[co2_cols], 1, fill_short_gaps))
cat("Missing annual CO2 values before:", sum(is.na(co2_clean[co2_cols])), "\n")
cat("Missing annual CO2 values after limited interpolation:", sum(is.na(co2_interpolated[co2_cols])), "\n")
cat("Estimated values:", sum(is.na(co2_clean[co2_cols])) - sum(is.na(co2_interpolated[co2_cols])), "\n")
```

## Check outliers using boxplots

I used boxplots to check numerical variables. I left out Rank because it is a position, not a measurement. I did not remove unusual values without evidence of an error.

```{r}
quantitative <- pop_clean[sapply(pop_clean, is.numeric)]
quantitative$Rank <- NULL
outlier_summary <- data.frame(
 Variable=names(quantitative),
 Potential_outliers=sapply(quantitative, function(x) length(boxplot.stats(x)$out)))
knitr::kable(outlier_summary, caption="Population outliers by IQR rule")
for (v in names(quantitative)) {
  print(ggplot(quantitative, aes(y=.data[[v]])) +
    geom_boxplot(fill="lightblue", outlier.color="firebrick") +
    labs(title=paste("Boxplot:",v), y=v, x=NULL) + theme_minimal())
}
```

For the CO2 dataset, inspect the distribution of the observed 2019 emissions per person.

```{r}
ggplot(co2_clean, aes(y=X2019)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill="lightgreen", na.rm=TRUE, outlier.color="firebrick") +
  labs(title="2019 CO2 per capita: potential outliers", y="Metric tons per person") + theme_minimal()
```

## Summary statistics

```{r}
area_col <- grep("^Area", names(pop_clean), value=TRUE)[1]
density_col <- grep("^Density", names(pop_clean), value=TRUE)[1]
summary(pop_clean[c("X2022.Population",area_col,density_col,"Growth.Rate","World.Population.Percentage")])
summary(co2_clean$X2019)
```

# Create a projected 2030 population variable

I estimated the 2030 population using the 2022 population and growth rate. I assumed the growth rate stays the same for eight years.

```{r}
stopifnot(all(pop_clean$Growth.Rate > 0))
pop_clean$Projected_2030 <- round(pop_clean$X2022.Population * exp(8*log(pop_clean$Growth.Rate)))
projection <- pop_clean[order(-pop_clean$Projected_2030), c("Country.Territory","X2022.Population","Growth.Rate","Projected_2030")]
knitr::kable(head(projection, 15), caption="Top 15 projected populations for 2030")
```

# Population and CO2 trends

## Top ten countries in 2022

```{r}
top10 <- head(pop_clean[order(-pop_clean$X2022.Population),],10)
knitr::kable(top10[c("Country.Territory","X2022.Population")], caption="Top ten populations in 2022")
ggplot(top10, aes(x=reorder(Country.Territory,X2022.Population),y=X2022.Population)) +
 geom_col(fill="steelblue") + coord_flip() +
 labs(title="Ten most populous countries in 2022",x="Country",y="Population") + theme_minimal()
```

## Top ten population trends (available benchmark years, 1990–2022)

```{r}
pop_years <- c(1990,2000,2010,2015,2020,2022)
pop_long <- do.call(rbind,lapply(pop_years,function(y) data.frame(
 Country=top10$Country.Territory,Year=y,Population=top10[[paste0("X",y,".Population")]])))
ggplot(pop_long,aes(Year,Population,color=Country,group=Country)) +
 geom_line(linewidth=.8) + geom_point(size=1.2) +
 scale_x_continuous(breaks=pop_years) +
 labs(title="Population trends: top ten countries",subtitle="Lines connect available benchmark years only",y="Population") + theme_minimal()
```

## Top ten CO2 per-capita trends, 1990–2019

I matched countries using their country codes because some country names are written differently in the two files.

```{r}
merged <- merge(pop_clean,co2_clean,by.x="CCA3",by.y="country_code",all.x=TRUE)
merged_interp <- merge(pop_clean,co2_interpolated,by.x="CCA3",by.y="country_code",all.x=TRUE)
cat("Population rows without a matching CO2 country code:",sum(is.na(merged$X1990) & is.na(merged$Country.Name)),"\n")
co2_top <- merged[merged$CCA3 %in% top10$CCA3,]
co2_long <- do.call(rbind,lapply(co2_years,function(y) data.frame(
 Country=co2_top$Country.Territory,Year=y,CO2=co2_top[[paste0("X",y)]])))
ggplot(co2_long,aes(Year,CO2,color=Country,group=Country)) +
 geom_line(linewidth=.8,na.rm=TRUE) +
 labs(title="CO2 per person: ten most populous countries",subtitle="Observed data; gaps are not treated as zero",y="Metric tons per person") + theme_minimal()
```

## Check the effect of filling short gaps

```{r}
obs <- co2_clean[co2_clean$country_code %in% top10$CCA3,]
imp <- co2_interpolated[co2_interpolated$country_code %in% top10$CCA3,]
cat("Observed missing top-ten country-year values:",sum(is.na(obs[co2_cols])),"\n")
cat("Missing after limited interpolation:",sum(is.na(imp[co2_cols])),"\n")
```

# Correlation analysis

## Area, density, growth rate and world population share

```{r}
cor_cols <- c(area_col,density_col,"Growth.Rate","World.Population.Percentage")
cor_matrix <- cor(pop_clean[cor_cols],use="complete.obs")
knitr::kable(round(cor_matrix,3),caption="Pearson correlation matrix")
cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix))
names(cor_long) <- c("Variable1","Variable2","Correlation")
ggplot(cor_long,aes(Variable1,Variable2,fill=Correlation)) +
 geom_tile(color="white") + geom_text(aes(label=sprintf("%.2f",Correlation)),size=3) +
 scale_fill_gradient2(low="steelblue",mid="white",high="firebrick",midpoint=0,limits=c(-1,1)) +
 coord_equal() + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=40,hjust=1)) +
 labs(title="Correlation heatmap",x=NULL,y=NULL)
```

## 2022 population versus observed 2019 CO2 per capita

```{r}
paired <- merged[complete.cases(merged[c("X2022.Population","X2019")]),]
cat("Paired observations:",nrow(paired),"\n")
cat("Pearson:",cor(paired$X2022.Population,paired$X2019),"\n")
cat("Spearman:",cor(paired$X2022.Population,paired$X2019,method="spearman"),"\n")
fit <- lm(X2019 ~ X2022.Population,data=paired)
summary(fit)
ggplot(paired,aes(X2022.Population,X2019)) +
 geom_point(alpha=.6,color="steelblue") + geom_smooth(method="lm",se=TRUE,color="firebrick") +
 labs(title="Population versus CO2 per person",x="2022 population",y="2019 CO2 (metric tons per person)") + theme_minimal()
```

## Check the regression results

```{r}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(fit,which=1)
plot(fit,which=2)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
paired_interp <- merged_interp[complete.cases(merged_interp[c("X2022.Population","X2019")]),]
cat("Observed-data Pearson:",cor(paired$X2022.Population,paired$X2019),"\n")
cat("Interpolated-series Pearson:",cor(paired_interp$X2022.Population,paired_interp$X2019),"\n")
```

The CO2 values are per person, not total emissions. I used the correlation and regression to look for a pattern, not to prove that population causes emissions.

# Compare continents

I compared continents using the available 2019 CO2 values. These are emissions per person, so adding them does not give total emissions for a continent.

```{r}
continent_sum <- aggregate(X2019 ~ Continent,data=paired,sum)
continent_mean <- aggregate(X2019 ~ Continent,data=paired,mean)
continent_count <- aggregate(X2019 ~ Continent,data=paired,length)
continent_summary <- Reduce(function(a,b)merge(a,b,by="Continent"),list(continent_sum,continent_mean,continent_count))
names(continent_summary) <- c("Continent","Sum_country_per_capita","Mean_country_per_capita","Countries_observed")
continent_summary <- continent_summary[order(-continent_summary$Sum_country_per_capita),]
knitr::kable(continent_summary,digits=3,caption="2019 country-level CO2 per-capita indicators by continent")
ggplot(continent_summary,aes(reorder(Continent,Sum_country_per_capita),Sum_country_per_capita)) +
 geom_col(fill="steelblue") + coord_flip() +
 labs(title="Sum of country-level per-capita CO2 values",subtitle="Not total continental CO2 emissions",x="Continent",y="Sum of per-capita indicators") + theme_minimal()
cat("First:",continent_summary$Continent[1],"\n")
cat("Third:",continent_summary$Continent[3],"value:",continent_summary$Sum_country_per_capita[3],"\n")
cat("Last:",tail(continent_summary$Continent,1),"value:",tail(continent_summary$Sum_country_per_capita,1),"\n")
```

# Conclusion

I found no missing values in the population dataset, but the CO2 dataset had some gaps. I kept valid outliers and used the available values for the main analysis. The 2030 figures are estimates, and the CO2 results should be interpreted carefully because they are per-person values from 2019.
